name: HTTP/2 connection fingerprint (Akamai)
plain: HTTP/2 settings, window updates and header order differ by browser and are readable by the server.
meaning: Akamai's fingerprint (Black Hat EU 2017) joins SETTINGS values, WINDOW_UPDATE, PRIORITY frames and pseudo-header order. Chrome sends m,a,s,p, Firefox m,p,a,s and Safari m,s,p,a; Go and Python clients differ visibly.

web.api: HTTP/2 frame capture at the edge

limits.headline: Can tell which browser or tool you use from how your connection starts up
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens as your browser connects to the site
can: Compare connection settings and header order with known browsers
Tell Chrome, Firefox and Safari apart from each other
Spot scripts and bots whose settings look different
cannot: Know your name or account from it
Tell two people on the same browser apart

story.what_it_is: The way your browser opens a modern web connection leaves a signature the site can read.
story.for_you: You never see it. When you connect, your browser sends settings in a pattern that is almost the same for every copy of Chrome, Safari or Firefox. A site can tell the real thing from a lookalike script.
story.for_makers: Security vendors like Akamai and Cloudflare use it to tell real browsers from bots that fake a browser name. It catches many scrapers and card testing tools. It also adds to a fingerprint that is hard to change.

use_cases.example: A bot defense compares the connection pattern with the claimed browser and challenges mismatches.
A retailer stops price scrapers that pretend to be Chrome.
A game launcher site blocks automated tools that buy limited items.
An ad platform removes fake traffic from automation tools.
A bank adds the connection pattern to its fraud score at login.
A traffic analyst uses it to name the real browser share.

technical_bounds: Same fingerprint across browser versions sharing an engine

refs.label: Shuster et al., Passive Fingerprinting of HTTP/2 Clients (Black Hat EU 2017)
